style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings. Ecclesiastes uses Elohim throughout — the divine name YHWH never appears in the book and is never inserted.
chapterNote: The Preacher walks out of the study and into the street, and what he sees there is worse than futility: it is cruelty. The oppressed weep and no one comforts them -- the terrible line falls twice in one verse. Then a gallery of solitary men: the worker driven by envy of his neighbor, the fool consuming himself in idleness, and, most pitiable, the man alone with no son, no brother, no partner, heaping up riches with no one to ask him the question that would set him free: for whom am I doing this? Against that loneliness the chapter sets its warmest passage in the book -- two are better than one, for lifting, for warmth, for defense, and a cord of three strands is not quickly snapped. The closing parable of the poor wise youth who rises from prison to the throne, only to be forgotten by the next generation, brings even popularity and political hope under the same verdict: vapor, and a chasing after wind.

1.text: Then I turned back and looked at all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and there were the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; power sat in the hand of their oppressors, and still they had no comforter.
1.amp: So I returned [shub], and considered [raah] all the oppressions that are done [asah] under the sun [shemesh]: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed [ashaq -- exploited, extorted], and they had no comforter [nacham]; and on the hand of their oppressors there was power [koach]; but they had no comforter.
1.notes: ashaq (H6231) is oppression by extortion, the strong squeezing the weak, and koach (H3581) the raw power backing it. 'No comforter' falls twice in the one verse; nacham, the comfort-word, is exactly what Isaiah later promises God Himself will bring (cf. Isaiah 40:1).

2.text: So I congratulated the dead, those already gone, more than the living who are still walking through it;
2.amp: Wherefore I praised [shabach -- commended, counted happy] the dead which are already [kebar] dead more than the living [chay] which are yet alive.
2.notes: shabach (H7623) is to commend or count fortunate: gallows congratulation, spoken from inside the observation of verse 1. The dead are past being oppressed; the chay (H2416), the living, are still in reach of it.

3.text: And better off than both of them is the one who has never yet existed, who has never had to watch the evil work that is done under the sun.
3.amp: Yea, better [tov] is he than both they, which has not yet been, who has not seen [raah] the evil [ra] work [maaseh] that is done [asah] under the sun.
3.notes: The darkest rung of the ladder: dead, living, never-born, ranked in that order (cf. Job 3:11-16 for the same grief-logic). ra (H7451) is evil in its active, injuring sense; it is the seeing of it that the unborn are spared.

4.text: Then I looked at all the toil and all the skillful achievement of men, and saw that it runs on the envy of a man toward his neighbor. This also is vapor and a chasing after wind.
4.amp: Again, I considered [raah] all travail [amal], and every skillful work [maaseh -- 'all the rightness of work', the KJV margin], that for this a man [ish] is envied [qinah -- jealousy, rivalry] of his neighbour [rea]. This is also vapor [hebel] and vexation [reuth] of spirit [ruach].
4.notes: qinah (H7068) is jealousy and rivalry: the engine under the economy is not love of the work but the sideways glance at the rea (H7453), the neighbor. Diagnosed at the root, even excellence is competitive envy, and so hebel (H1892).

5.text: The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh away.
5.amp: The fool [kesil] folds [chabaq -- clasps] his hands together, and eats [akal] his own flesh [basar].
5.notes: chabaq (H2263), the embrace-word of chapter 3, turned inward: the kesil (H3684) hugs his own idle hands. Eating his basar (H1320), his own flesh, is self-consumption -- refusing the rat race by refusing all work is no escape, only a slower ruin.

6.text: Better one open palm filled, and quietness with it, than two fists full of toil and a chasing after wind.
6.amp: Better [tov] is a handful [kaph -- the open palm] with quietness [nachat -- rest, calm], than both the hands [chophen -- the clenched double-fistful] full [melo] with travail [amal] and vexation [reuth] of spirit [ruach].
6.notes: The Hebrew sets two different hands against each other: kaph (H3709), the single open palm, versus the doubled grasping fists (H2651). nachat (H5183) is settled quietness -- the proverb prices peace into the wage and finds half with rest worth more than double without it.

7.text: Then I turned again, and I saw another vapor under the sun:
7.amp: Then I returned [shub], and I saw [raah] vapor [hebel] under the sun [shemesh].
7.notes: shub (H7725), to turn back: the survey resumes, and the next exhibit is already announced as hebel (H1892) before it is described.

8.text: There is a man all alone, without a second, without son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eye is never satisfied with riches. He never asks, 'For whom am I toiling and starving my own soul of good?' This also is vapor; indeed, it is a miserable business.
8.amp: There is [yesh] one [echad] alone, and there is not a second; yea, he has neither child [ben] nor brother [ach]: yet is there no end [qets] of all his labour [amal]; neither is his eye [ayin] satisfied [saba] with riches; neither says he, 'For whom do I labour [amel], and bereave [chaser -- deprive, leave lacking] my soul [nephesh] of good [tov]?' This is also vapor [hebel], yea, it is a sore [ra] travail [inyan].
8.notes: echad (H259), one, with no second: the loneliest figure in the book, wealth without a single heir or witness. chaser (H2637) is to leave lacking -- he bereaves his own nephesh (H5315) -- and the unasked 'for whom?' is the question that would have freed him. inyan (H6045), the business-word again: a miserable business indeed.

9.text: Two are better than one, because together they have a good return for their toil.
9.amp: Two are better [tov] than one [echad]; because they have [yesh] a good reward [sakar -- wages] for their labour [amal].
9.notes: The answer to verse 8 begins. The reward-word (H7939, sakar) is the laborer's wage: partnership actually changes the arithmetic of toil, paying out what solitude never could.

10.text: For if they fall, the one will lift his companion up; but how it goes hard for the one who falls alone, with no second there to raise him.
10.amp: For if they fall [naphal], the one [echad] will lift up [qum -- raise to standing] his fellow [chaver -- companion, friend]: but woe [iy] to him that is alone when he falls; for he has not another to help him up [qum].
10.notes: chaver (H2270) is the companion bound by association, and qum (H6965) the verb of standing someone back on his feet. iy (H337), 'woe', is a cry of pity rather than doom: the fall is the same for both men; the difference is who is lying there alone.

11.text: Again, if two lie down together, they keep each other warm; but how can one keep warm alone?
11.amp: Again [gam], if two lie together [shakab], then they have heat [chamam -- grow warm]: but how can one [echad] be warm alone?
11.notes: chamam (H2552), to grow warm: the picture is the shared cloak of travelers on a cold night (cf. Exodus 22:26-27 on the cloak as covering by night). Body heat, like the wage of verse 9, only multiplies when shared.

12.text: And though an attacker may overpower one man, two together will stand against him; and a cord of three strands is not quickly snapped.
12.amp: And if one prevail [taqaph -- overpower] against him, two shall withstand [amad -- stand firm against] him; and a threefold cord [chut -- thread, line] is not quickly [meherah] broken [nathaq -- snapped, torn apart].
12.notes: amad (H5975), to stand one's ground: defense is the third gain of partnership, after wages and warmth. The chut (H2339), the cord, climbs from one strand to two to three -- and the proverb leaves the third strand unnamed, an open invitation to count God into the weave.

13.text: Better a poor but wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.
13.amp: Better [tov] is a poor and a wise [chakam] youth than an old [zaqen] and foolish [kesil] king [melek], who knows [yada] no more how to be admonished [zahar -- warned, made to shine with light].
13.notes: zahar (H2094) is to warn or enlighten; the KJV margin reads 'who knoweth not to be admonished'. The ranking is deliberately shocking for a royal author: poverty with teachable chokmah outranks a crown grown deaf, for the kesil (H3684) here wears purple.

14.text: For the youth came up out of the prison house to reign, even though in the old king's own kingdom he had been born poor.
14.amp: For out of the prison [asar -- the house of the bound] he comes [yatsa] to reign [malak]; whereas also he that is born [yalad] in his kingdom [malkuth] becomes poor [rush -- destitute].
14.notes: asar (H631) is to bind: the youth rises from the house of bonds to the throne, a Joseph-shaped ascent (cf. Genesis 41:14, 41). The verse's mirrored halves swap prison for palace and riches for rags; under the sun the wheel turns both ways.

15.text: I watched all the living who walk under the sun side with the second youth, the successor who would stand up in the old king's place.
15.amp: I considered [raah] all the living [chay] which walk [halak] under the sun [shemesh], with the second youth that shall stand up [amad] in his stead.
15.notes: The crowd's affection has already moved on, to a 'second' youth, the next successor in line. amad (H5975), to stand up in another's place: the cycle of succession is itself a parade, and everyone walking under the sun falls in behind the newest face.

16.text: There was no end to all the people, all those he came to lead; yet those who come after will find no joy in him. Surely this also is vapor and a striving after wind.
16.amp: There is no end [qets] of all the people [am], even of all that have been before [panim] them: they also that come after [acharon] shall not rejoice [samach] in him. Surely this also is vapor [hebel] and vexation [raayon] of spirit [ruach].
16.notes: The crowd is numberless, qets (H7093), without end, and its memory is just as boundless in forgetting: the acharon (H314), the generation after, will not samach (H8055), rejoice, in yesterday's deliverer. Even the best succession story evaporates into hebel (H1892).
